entries.type: conjunctive adverb (Latin) of comparative inference; also attributive, as an adjective before a noun (an a fortiori argument)
entries.register: formal; Latin — the register of judicial opinions, briefs, law reviews, and analytic philosophy
entries.clause: sentence adverbial marking its clause as following with even greater force from what the previous clause already granted
entries.pattern: [Independent clause]; a fortiori, [independent clause]. · [Independent clause]. A fortiori, [independent clause]. · If [weaker case], then a fortiori [stronger case]. · [main clause], and a fortiori [phrase]. · an a fortiori [argument / case / reason] (attributive).
entries.punctuation: Comma after it when it opens a clause. Between two independent clauses it is an adverb, not a conjunction, so it takes a semicolon or a period in front of it — a comma there is a comma splice: ✗ The rule bars a dinner, a fortiori it bars a car. ✓ The rule bars a dinner; a fortiori, it bars a car. Only and can carry it across with a comma (…, and a fortiori…). No commas in the attributive use. Set it in roman in American legal writing; it has been naturalized long enough not to need italics.
entries.meaning: Latin for "from the stronger [argument]": it says that a point already conceded in a weaker case must hold with greater force in a stronger one. It is the Latin name of the how much more frame, and the difference is what each one does with the move — how much more asks a rhetorical question, while a fortiori asserts a conclusion, which is why briefs and philosophy papers use it where a sermon uses the English. An American reader meets it in court opinions, appellate briefs, and academic argument, and essentially nowhere else; in ordinary prose all the more so carries the same idea without the Latin.
examples: If a warrant is required to search a car, then a fortiori one is required to search a home.
The statute bars a legislator from accepting a fifty-dollar dinner; a fortiori, it bars accepting a car.
Congress may regulate the sale of the drug; a fortiori, it may regulate its manufacture.
She had no duty to volunteer the information, and a fortiori no duty to repeat it.
The court found the weaker record in Ramirez insufficient, and this record is thinner still — an a fortiori case if there ever was one.
If a grown adult could not have understood the waiver, a fortiori a fourteen-year-old could not.
related: how much more / how much less

entries.type: correlative comparative frame (subordinating), negative-polarity — it needs a negative, a question, or another non-affirmative context earlier in the sentence
entries.clause: adverbial clause of comparison (paired denial)
entries.pattern: [negative clause] any more than [clause]. · [negative clause] any more than [noun phrase] (elliptical). · Not [X] any more than [Y]. · [question] any more than [clause]?
entries.punctuation: No comma before any more than, and none inside the frame.
entries.meaning: The negative-polarity form of no more … than: it denies the main clause and the compared clause in one stroke, so I can't rebuild a transmission any more than I can land a plane says that both are beyond me. It cannot stand in a plain positive sentence — something non-affirmative (not, never, hardly, or a question) has to license it. Keep the two words apart: any more here is a degree phrase, not the adverb anymore meaning "these days."
examples: I can't rebuild a transmission any more than I can land a plane.
She doesn't set the schedule any more than the rest of us do.
A new logo won't fix the company any more than fresh paint fixes a cracked foundation.
He never asked for this any more than you did.
Nobody enjoys the paperwork any more than the inspectors do.
Does a title make him an expert any more than a uniform makes me a pilot?

entries.term: how much more / how much less
entries.respell: how much MOR, how much LESS
entries.type: rhetorical comparative frame (a fortiori) — a wh- degree phrase heading an elliptical clause, not a plain subordinator
entries.clause: exclamatory or interrogative comparative clause, usually elliptical, hanging off a clause that supplies the standard
entries.pattern: If [clause], how much more [phrase]? · [clause]; how much less [phrase]. · How much more [adj/adv] [noun phrase] [verb phrase]! · [clause] — how much more so [phrase].
entries.punctuation: A comma or a semicolon at the seam, because the second half is a separate rhetorical move rather than a completion of the first. A question mark or an exclamation point at the end, depending on whether it is put as a question or an exclamation. No comma inside the frame.
entries.meaning: The a-fortiori frame: it takes a case the reader has already granted and argues that the point holds with even greater force in the second case. How much more pushes the conclusion up from a small case to a large one, and how much less pushes it down after a negative. The second half is almost always elliptical, and it is a rhetorical question — no answer is expected or wanted.
examples: If one missed payment dents your credit, how much more a foreclosure?
They wouldn't listen to their own auditor; how much less to a stranger with a spreadsheet.
If the draft was too long, how much more the version with the appendices.
Children notice when adults are tired — how much more when adults are angry.
If we can't keep one office running, how much less a national network of them.
How much more difficult the climb becomes once the weather turns.

entries.type: correlative comparative frame (subordinating)
entries.clause: adverbial clause of comparison
entries.pattern: [X] is no less [adj] than [Y] (is). · [clause] [verb] no less than [clause]. · No less than [quantity / name] [verb phrase]. · [X] is no less a [noun] than [Y].
entries.punctuation: No comma before than. No comma inside the frame.
entries.meaning: Asserts that the first term measures up to the second, usually with the rhetorical suggestion that people underrate it. Where no more … than denies the quality of both terms at once, no less … than affirms it of both, and the bare no less than before a number or a name means "and that is a lot" rather than "at most."
examples: The sequel is no less ambitious than the original.
Her second novel was no less well received than her first.
He was no less surprised than I was to see her name on the list.
No less than the mayor herself showed up to cut the ribbon.
The repairs will cost no less than they did last spring.
Two summers on a job site taught him no less than four years of classes had.
Losing the grant was no less a setback than losing the lease had been.

entries.type: correlative comparative frame (subordinating)
entries.register: neutral; the paired-denial frame is formal and rhetorical
entries.clause: adverbial clause of comparison
entries.pattern: [X] is no more [adj] than [Y] (is). · [X] is no more a [noun] than [Y] (is). · [clause] [verb] no more than [clause]. · [clause] [verb] no more than [quantity].
entries.punctuation: No comma before than.
entries.meaning: In its argument frame this denies the property of both terms together: He is no more a scientist than I am says neither of us is one. Learners regularly read it as an ordinary "less than" comparison; it is actually a paired denial, and the second term is chosen precisely because it is obviously false. Before a bare quantity it means simply "at most."
examples: A rented tux makes him no more a groom than a costume makes me a pilot.
The committee has no more authority here than the audience does.
She's no more to blame than you are.
It took no more than twenty minutes to change the tire.
He earns no more than he did five years ago.
That was no more an accident than the fire last spring.

entries.type: correlative
entries.register: formal to neutral; the fronted form is literary
entries.clause: adverbial clause of time built on a comparative frame
entries.pattern: No sooner [auxiliary] [subject] [verb] than [clause]. · [subject] had no sooner [past participle] than [clause].
entries.punctuation: No comma at the seam — than joins the halves directly. Fronting No sooner forces subject–auxiliary inversion: No sooner had we sat down than…, never No sooner we had sat down.
entries.meaning: Formally a comparison, semantically pure sequence: it says the second event followed the first immediately. Because the frame is comparative, the second half must be than; no sooner … when is the commonest error in this construction, and it comes from confusing it with hardly … when and scarcely … when, which do take when.
examples: No sooner had we sat down than the fire alarm went off.
No sooner did the rain stop than the mosquitoes came out.
She had no sooner hung up than the phone rang again.
No sooner was the ink dry than they wanted changes.
We had no sooner unpacked than the landlord called about a leak.
No sooner had the news broken than the stock dropped nine points.

entries.type: subordinating; also works as a quasi-coordinator
entries.clause: adverbial clause of preference and substitution; also links two parallel phrases
entries.pattern: Rather than [bare infinitive / -ing], [main clause]. · [main clause] rather than [bare infinitive]. · [X] rather than [Y] (two matching phrases). · [subject] would rather [bare infinitive] than [bare infinitive].
entries.punctuation: Comma after a fronted rather than phrase. No comma when it links two parallel elements inside a clause. Commas on both sides only when it is a parenthetical afterthought.
entries.meaning: Marks the rejected alternative. Its nearest neighbor is instead of, and they take different complements: rather than takes a bare infinitive when the main clause has one (Rather than pay, we walked out), while instead of requires -ing (Instead of paying, we walked out). Whatever sits on the two sides of rather than must be the same kind of phrase.
examples: Rather than argue about it, I just paid the fee.
We took the train rather than fly.
She sees it as a delay rather than a defeat.
Rather than wait for approval, the team shipped a draft.
He wants honest feedback rather than praise.
The problem is structural rather than personal.

entries.type: subordinating
entries.clause: adverbial clause of preference; also a plain comparison of time
entries.pattern: [subject] would [bare infinitive] sooner than [bare infinitive] (preference). · [subject] 'd sooner [bare infinitive] than [bare infinitive]. · Sooner than [bare infinitive], [main clause]. · [main clause] sooner than [clause] (literal time).
entries.punctuation: No comma before sooner than. Comma after a fronted Sooner than phrase.
entries.meaning: The emphatic sibling of rather than: it states a preference the speaker treats as obvious, usually a refusal dressed up as a choice. It also has a literal time reading (She got here sooner than we expected), and the bare infinitive after it is the signal that you are in the preference sense rather than the time sense.
examples: I'd quit sooner than work another holiday weekend.
He'd sell the house sooner than ask his brother for money.
Sooner than sit through that meeting again, I'll take the early flight.
The package arrived sooner than the tracking page promised.
She'd walk home in the rain sooner than call a cab.
They finished sooner than anyone thought possible.

entries.type: subordinating (comparative); prepositional in the than me usage
entries.clause: adverbial clause of comparison, attached to a comparative word earlier in the sentence
entries.pattern: [clause + comparative adj/adv] than [clause]. · [clause + more / less / fewer + noun] than [clause]. · [clause + comparative] than [noun phrase] (elliptical: than me, than last year's). · [clause + other / rather / sooner / else / different] than [phrase].
entries.punctuation: No comma before than in a comparison. A comma appears only when the than phrase is a deliberate afterthought set off from the rest of the sentence.
entries.meaning: The workhorse of unequal comparison. It cannot start a comparison by itself — something earlier must license it, either a comparative form (taller, more slowly, fewer) or one of a short list of trigger words (other, rather, sooner, else, different). The clause after it is almost always elliptical, which is where the case argument lives: taller than I (am) is the conservative written form and taller than me the ordinary spoken one, and both are defensible in American English. One last thing it is not: then. Than compares; then tells time or draws a consequence. They sound alike in unstressed speech — both reduce to /ðən/ — and that is exactly why the misspelling is the single commonest error in the category. Test it by stressing the word: if the sentence still means "at that time," you want then.
examples: She finished the course faster than anyone expected.
This apartment costs more than our last one did.
There were fewer people at the hearing than the organizers had hoped.
He knows the neighborhood better than I do.
I'd rather drive than sit in an airport for six hours.
The recipe calls for something other than butter.
That's a bigger crowd than last year's.

entries.type: subordinating conjunction + relative pronoun
entries.clause: nonrestrictive relative clause built on a comparative
entries.pattern: [noun phrase], than whom [no one / few / nobody] [verb phrase], [rest of main clause]. · [noun phrase], than which [nothing / few / no + noun] [verb phrase], [rest of main clause]. · [noun phrase], than whom [subject] [verb] [no one / nothing] more, [rest of main clause].
entries.punctuation: Commas on both sides, always — the clause is supplementary, never restrictive. This is the one place in the than family where a comma stands directly before than.
entries.meaning: A fossilized formal construction, and the one place in modern English where than is unmistakably followed by the objective case — the historical argument for calling than a preposition. It reads as deliberately elevated and nearly always pairs with a negative that gives it superlative force (than whom no one, than which nothing).
examples: Dr. Reyes, than whom no one is better qualified, will chair the panel.
She studied under Kowalski, than whom the department has known no stricter grader.
The Chrysler Building, than which few American towers have aged better, still stops traffic.
He named his old editor, than whom he trusted no one more, as his literary executor.
The award went to Ellis, than whom the league has produced no steadier defender.

entries.ipa: /æz … əz/ — the first as carries the stress and stays full, the second reduces to /əz/
entries.type: correlative (equative comparison)
entries.clause: adverbial clause of comparison
entries.pattern: [clause] as [adj/adv] as [clause/phrase]. · [clause] not as [adj/adv] as [clause/phrase]. · as [adj] a(n) [noun] as [phrase]. · [clause] as much / as many [noun] as [clause]. · [clause] [twice / half / three times] as [adj/adv] as [phrase].
entries.punctuation: No commas anywhere inside the frame, in any of those orders.
entries.meaning: States that two things match on some scale. The trap is word order in the noun pattern: when a singular count noun is compared, the article jumps to the far side of the adjective — as fine a meal as I've had, not as a fine meal as I've had. No other English frame moves the article that way.
examples: The drive is as long as the flight once you count security.
She's as good a manager as the company has ever had.
Bring as many chairs as you can fit in the car.
It's not as cold today as it was yesterday.
He explained it as clearly as anyone could have.
The copy reads as well as the original did.

entries.type: correlative
entries.clause: adverbial clause of comparison with a resumptive main clause
entries.pattern: As [clause], so [clause]. · Just as [clause], so (too) [clause].
entries.punctuation: Comma at the seam between the two halves. So opens the second half and often triggers inversion (so grows the tree, so too should writers rest).
entries.meaning: Sets up an analogy: as the first proposition goes, so goes the second. This is the elevated, written-out version of the comparison that ordinary speech makes with just like, and it belongs in sermons, editorials, and formal argument rather than conversation.
examples: As the twig is bent, so grows the tree.
Just as the coasts warmed early, so the interior followed a decade later.
As the harvest failed, so the price of bread climbed.
Just as athletes taper before a race, so too should writers rest before a deadline.
As a city treats its parks, so it treats its people.

entries.type: subordinating (compound) with a clause; prepositional with a noun phrase in the distance sense
entries.clause: adverbial clause of comparison and extent; also literal distance
entries.pattern: As far as [clause], [main clause]. · [main clause] as far as [clause]. · [main clause] as far as [noun phrase] (literal distance; prepositional). · As far as [noun phrase] is concerned / goes, [main clause]. · [main clause] as far as [noun phrase] is concerned / goes.
entries.punctuation: Comma after the clause whenever it is fronted (As far as I know, …). No comma when it follows the main clause — in the extent sense (He'll help as far as he's able) and in the literal-distance sense (The trail runs as far as the old fire tower) alike.
entries.meaning: Limits a claim to the reach of somebody's knowledge, authority, or physical distance. In edited American prose it should keep its verb: write as far as the budget is concerned, not the clipped as far as the budget, which is common in speech but still corrected in print. Its formal twin is insofar as.
examples: As far as I know, the office closes at four on Fridays.
The trail runs as far as the old fire tower.
As far as the budget is concerned, nothing has changed.
He'll help as far as he's able.
As far as anyone could tell, the machine was working fine.
You can see as far as the state line from up here.

entries.type: correlative (equative of preference)
entries.clause: adverbial clause of comparison expressing preference
entries.pattern: [subject] had as lief [bare infinitive] as [bare infinitive]. · [subject] would as lief [bare infinitive] as [bare infinitive]. · [subject] 'd as lief [bare infinitive] as not. · As lief [bare infinitive] as [bare infinitive] — [main clause].
entries.punctuation: No commas inside the frame.
entries.meaning: The Elizabethan ancestor of would just as soon. Lief is a dead adverb meaning "willingly" (the root survives in German lieb), and the frame claims equal willingness to do either thing — which in practice is a courteous refusal of the first. Note the verb the old idiom takes: had as lief, not would as lief, is what the printed texts have, and anything written this century should say I'd just as soon.
examples: I had as lief walk as wait an hour for the next bus.
He'd as lief pay the fine as argue with a clerk about it.
"I had as lief not be as live to be in awe of such a thing as I myself." — Julius Caesar
She would as lief have stayed home, and said so twice.
They'd as lief see the building torn down as watch it rot another decade.
I'd as lief not, if it's all the same to you.

entries.type: correlative (equative, count)
entries.clause: adverbial clause of comparison
entries.pattern: [clause] as many [plural noun] as [clause/phrase]. · [clause] as many of [noun phrase] as [clause]. · [clause] [twice / half / three times] as many [plural noun] as [phrase]. · As many as [number] [verb phrase]. · [clause] as many as [number].
entries.punctuation: No commas inside the frame.
entries.meaning: The countable half of the equative pair: as many as takes plural count nouns and as much as takes mass nouns, and mixing them (as much chairs) is one of the most visible learner errors in English. Standing alone before a number it means "up to — and that is a surprising number."
examples: Take as many forms as you need.
She's read as many of his books as I have.
As many as two hundred people were turned away at the door.
We didn't sell as many tickets as we did last spring.
Bring as many helpers as will fit in the van.
There were as many questions as there were answers.

entries.type: correlative (equative, degree)
entries.clause: adverbial clause of comparison; also an adverbial clause of concession
entries.pattern: [clause] as much as [clause/phrase]. · [clause] as much [mass noun] as [clause]. · [clause] [twice / half] as much [mass noun] as [phrase]. · As much as [clause], [main clause] (concessive). · [clause] as much as [quantity].
entries.punctuation: No comma in the degree sense. In the concessive sense the clause comes first and takes a comma after it: As much as I'd like to, I can't.
entries.meaning: Measures degree, or quantity of a mass noun. It leads a second life at the front of a sentence, where As much as I like her means "although I like her very much" — identical words, completely different job, and only position and the comma tell you which one you are reading. The formal equivalent of that concessive use is much as.
examples: He worries about the deadline as much as you do.
Pour in as much stock as the pan will hold.
As much as I'd like to help, I'm booked all week.
The repair cost as much as the car was worth.
She travels as much as her job allows.
As much as it hurt, quitting was the right call.

entries.type: correlative (equative) in the comparison sense; quasi-coordinator in the additive sense
entries.clause: adverbial clause of comparison (manner and degree); the additive sense links noun phrases instead
entries.pattern: [clause] as well as [clause]. · [clause] as well as [noun phrase]. · [X], as well as [Y], [verb phrase]. · As well as [-ing], [main clause].
entries.punctuation: No comma in the comparison sense. In the additive sense the commas depend on where the phrase sits: commas on both sides when it interrupts a subject and its verb (The manager, as well as the players, was fined), a comma after it when it is fronted (As well as teaching two sections, she advises the debate team), and no comma at all when it simply trails as the second item in a pair (They serve breakfast as well as lunch). Whichever way it is punctuated, it does not change the verb's number — was fined, singular, unlike and.
entries.meaning: Two grammars share these three words. As an equative it compares skill or quality: She plays as well as her teacher means she plays equally well. As a quasi-coordinator it means "in addition to," and that is the one that breaks agreement rules for learners, because unlike and it leaves the subject singular.
examples: He writes as well as anyone on the staff.
The new model handles as well as the one it replaced.
The coach, as well as two assistants, was suspended.
She speaks Portuguese as well as she speaks Spanish.
They serve breakfast as well as lunch.
The car stops as well as it did the day we bought it.
As well as teaching two sections, she advises the debate team.

entries.type: subordinating (compound)
entries.clause: adverbial clause of comparison and extent
entries.pattern: Insofar as [clause], [main clause]. · [main clause] insofar as [clause]. · [main clause] only insofar as [clause]. · [main clause] insofar as [noun phrase] is concerned (heavy; usually better as a clause).
entries.punctuation: Comma after the fronted clause; no comma when it follows the main clause.
entries.meaning: Restricts a statement to the degree that something holds — the legal-and-academic register of as far as. Its lookalike inasmuch as is a different conjunction meaning "because," and swapping the two reverses the logic of a sentence, so keep the -so- and the -as- straight: in-so-far measures extent, in-as-much gives a reason. Spell it closed up in American prose; the spaced in so far as is chiefly British, and insomuch as is rare enough now to read as an affectation.
examples: The clause applies insofar as state law permits.
Insofar as the data are reliable, the trend is real.
He supported the plan insofar as it protected existing tenants.
Insofar as anyone can judge from the outside, the merger went smoothly.
The theory holds insofar as the sample stays representative.

entries.type: subordinating (intensified equative and manner); also temporal
entries.clause: adverbial clause of comparison or manner; adverbial clause of time in the "at that moment" sense
entries.pattern: Just as [clause], [main clause]. · [main clause] just as [clause] (manner or time). · [clause] just as [adj/adv] as [phrase] (comparison). · Just as [clause], so (too) [clause] (formal correlative).
entries.punctuation: Comma after the fronted just as clause. No comma when it follows the main clause.
entries.meaning: Just sharpens as into three readings: comparison ("exactly as much as," just as expensive as), manner ("in precisely the way," just as I predicted), and time ("at the very moment," just as we sat down). Nothing in the words themselves distinguishes them — what follows decides, and a second as means you are in the comparison sense.
examples: Just as I predicted, the flight was delayed.
The used one is just as reliable as the new model.
She left the kitchen just as she'd found it.
Just as his father had, he went into teaching.
The power went out just as the game went to overtime.
Just as the recipe warns, the sauce broke when I raised the heat.

entries.type: correlative
entries.clause: adverbial clause of comparison (corrective)
entries.pattern: [X] is not so much [noun phrase] as [noun phrase]. · [X] is not so much [adj] as [adj]. · [clause] not so much [phrase] as [phrase]. · [clause] not so much because [clause] as because [clause]. · Not so much [phrase] as [phrase] — [main clause] (fronted, dash-linked).
entries.punctuation: No comma before as. The two compared elements have to be the same kind of phrase.
entries.meaning: Rejects one description and substitutes a better one — "less this, more that." It is the polite corrective: it concedes that the first label was a reasonable guess before replacing it, whereas rather than simply rules the first option out. Do not confuse it with the fixed phrase not so much as meaning "not even" (She didn't so much as glance at the menu), which has no second element at all.
examples: It's not so much a job as a calling.
The problem is not so much the cost as the timing.
She was not so much angry as disappointed.
What sank the project was not so much bad luck as bad planning.
He's not so much retired as between projects.
The bill stalled not so much because the votes weren't there as because nobody wanted to schedule the vote.
Not so much a renovation as a demolition — that's what the contractor delivered.

entries.type: correlative (equative, negative and interrogative contexts)
entries.clause: adverbial clause of comparison
entries.pattern: [subject] is not so [adj/adv] as [clause/phrase]. · Is [subject] so [adj] as [clause]? (interrogative). · [clause] so [adj] as to [bare infinitive]. · [subject] didn't so much as [bare infinitive] (= not even). · Nothing / no one is so [adj] as [noun phrase].
entries.punctuation: No commas inside the frame.
entries.meaning: The older negative equative. Modern American English says not as … as nearly everywhere, and not so … as survives mainly in careful prose and in fixed phrases (not so much as a thank-you, so far as I can tell, so kind as to). Do not confuse it with the purpose marker so as to or the result frame so … that, which are different constructions that happen to start with the same word. So changes word class as it moves, and only one of its jobs takes a comma. Here it is a degree adverb sitting inside an equative frame, and nothing in the frame is punctuated. In It was late, so we left it is a coordinating conjunction joining two independent clauses, and that one takes a comma before it. In so that they'd hear us it opens a purpose clause; in so tired it is a bare intensifier; in So, where were we? it is a discourse marker. Sort out which so you have before you reach for any punctuation.
examples: The second act is not so strong as the first.
He isn't so young as he looks.
She didn't so much as glance at the menu.
Would you be so kind as to hold the door?
Nothing is so useless as a meeting that could have been an email.

entries.type: subordinating (equative)
entries.clause: adverbial clause of comparison; also a comparison complement after be
entries.pattern: [X] is the same as [Y]. · [X] is the same [noun] as [Y / clause]. · [main clause] the same as [clause]. · [X] is the same [noun] that [clause] (relative — that very one). · Same as [noun phrase] — [main clause] (clipped, informal).
entries.punctuation: No comma before as.
entries.meaning: Asserts identity rather than resemblance. The choice between as and that after same changes the meaning: the same house as we rented means one like it, while the same house that we rented means literally that house — as compares two things, that opens a relative clause about one of them.
examples: The chili tastes the same as my uncle's.
He wore the same coat as the man in the photograph.
Same as always — coffee, black, no sugar.
Filing online works the same as mailing the form.
She ordered the same as I did.
Nothing looked the same as it had before the renovation.

entries.type: subordinating (compound)
entries.clause: adverbial clause of extent and degree; also proportion
entries.pattern: [main clause] to the degree that [clause]. · To the degree that [clause], [main clause]. · [main clause] only to the degree that [clause]. · [main clause] to the extent that [clause] (the commoner twin).
entries.punctuation: Comma after the clause when it is fronted; no comma when it trails the main clause.
entries.meaning: Ties the truth of the main clause to how much of something is the case — plain-English insofar as. Keep it clear of the result frame to such a degree that, which looks almost identical and points the other way: this one measures a condition, that one reports a consequence. In American prose to the extent that is the default, and to the degree that is what you reach for when extent is already doing work elsewhere in the sentence.
examples: The policy helps renters to the degree that landlords actually register their units.
To the degree that the forecast is reliable, we should move the ceremony indoors.
He is responsible to the degree that he signed off on the numbers.
To the degree that anyone can plan for a flood, the town had planned.
The warranty covers the repair only to the degree that the damage wasn't deliberate.
Test scores predict college success to the degree that they measure preparation rather than money.

entries.type: conjunctive adverb of resemblance; prepositional in the heavier analogously to
entries.register: formal; academic, mathematical, scientific, and legal
entries.clause: sentence adverbial introducing a parallel case that runs the same way as the one just described
entries.pattern: [Independent clause]; analogously, [independent clause]. · [Independent clause]. Analogously, [independent clause]. · [main clause], and analogously [clause]. · [subject], analogously, [verb phrase]. · [main clause] analogously to [noun phrase] (prepositional, heavy).
entries.punctuation: Comma after it when it opens a sentence or a clause, and commas on both sides when it sits inside one. Between two independent clauses it is an adverb, so it needs a semicolon or a period in front of it — a comma there is a splice: ✗ The odd case runs by induction, analogously the even case does too. ✓ The odd case runs by induction; analogously, the even case does too. No comma in the prepositional analogously to.
entries.meaning: The technical register's similarly: it claims that the second case is built the same way as the first, point for point, rather than merely resembling it. That is what separates it from its everyday neighbors — similarly asserts a likeness and likewise only adds a second item, while analogously says the structure carries over, which is why it belongs to proofs, protocols, and doctrinal argument. It sounds pretentious the moment all you mean is "also."
examples: The proof for the odd case runs by induction; analogously, the even case follows from the same lemma.
Sodium reacts violently with water. Analogously, potassium does, only faster.
Federal courts read the exemption narrowly; analogously, most state courts have read their own versions the same way.
Wages track productivity in manufacturing, and analogously in freight.
A vaccine trains the immune system before there is an infection. Analogously, a fire drill trains a building's occupants before there is smoke.
The second experiment was designed analogously to the first, with temperature held constant instead of pressure.

entries.type: subordinating (manner and comparison); the same word also subordinates time and cause, and is a preposition in the role sense (as a teacher)
entries.register: neutral to formal in the manner sense
entries.clause: adverbial clause of manner or comparison; adverbial clause of time or cause in its other senses; prepositional phrase in the role sense
entries.pattern: [main clause] as [clause]. · As [clause], [main clause]. · [main clause], as [clause] (supplementary comment). · as + [past participle / adjective] (reduced: as expected, as noted above). · As [noun phrase], [main clause] (role; prepositional: As a teacher, she…).
entries.punctuation: No comma when the as clause follows the main clause and states manner: Do as I say. Comma when it is fronted (As I mentioned, the deposit is due Friday) and comma before it when it trails as a comment on the whole sentence rather than on the verb (The bill passed, as everyone expected). That comma is the only thing separating the two readings of She left as I asked: without it, in the way I asked; with it, and I had asked her to.
entries.meaning: The neutral manner subordinator, meaning "in the way that." It is the always-safe alternative to like, and unlike like it takes a full clause with no objection from anyone. Watch the overload: the same three letters also mark time (as we walked), cause (as it was late), and role (as a teacher, she…), and only context sorts them out — which is exactly why as is one of the hardest words in English for learners.
examples: Fold the paper as the diagram shows.
As I mentioned on the phone, the deposit is due Friday.
Leave the room as you found it.
She dressed as her mother had taught her.
The bill passed, as everyone expected.
Season the sauce as you like.

entries.type: subordinating (compound)
entries.clause: adverbial clause of manner and comparison, often hypothetical
entries.pattern: [main clause] as if [clause]. · [look / sound / feel / smell / seem] as if [clause]. · [main clause] as if to [verb phrase]. · As if [clause / reduced phrase], [main clause]. · As if! (standalone retort, informal).
entries.punctuation: No comma before as if when it follows the main clause. Comma after the clause when it is fronted.
entries.meaning: Introduces an unreal or unverified comparison — how something looks, sounds, feels, or seems. Mood matters: when the comparison is contrary to fact, careful writing keeps the past subjunctive (as if he were sorry), and when the situation may well be true, the indicative is normal (It looks as if the flight is on time).
examples: He talks as if he owns the place.
She looked as if she hadn't slept in days.
It smells in here as if something's burning.
The dog tilted its head as if to ask a question.
As if nothing had happened, he sat down and ordered lunch.
It sounds as if they're going to reschedule.

entries.type: subordinating (compound)
entries.clause: adverbial clause of manner and comparison, often hypothetical
entries.pattern: [main clause] as though [clause]. · [look/sound/feel/seem] as though [clause]. · [main clause] as though to [verb phrase]. · As though [clause / reduced phrase], [main clause].
entries.punctuation: No comma before as though when it follows the main clause. Comma after a fronted as though clause or reduced phrase: As though on cue, the lights came back on.
entries.meaning: The near-twin of as if, and the two are genuinely interchangeable in meaning. The only reliable difference is texture: as though reads a shade more literary and is slightly favored after verbs of feeling and appearance (It felt as though hours had passed), while as if dominates speech and owns the fixed retort As if!
examples: She spoke as though the decision had already been made.
It felt as though hours had passed in that waiting room.
He shrugged as though the whole thing bored him.
The house looked as though no one had lived there in years.
As though on cue, the lights came back on.
They acted as though we hadn't been standing there for an hour.

entries.type: subordinating (fossilized manner clause)
entries.clause: adverbial clause of manner, elliptical and supplementary
entries.pattern: [main clause], as who should say [reported words]. · [main clause], as who should say, "[direct speech]." · [main clause], as much as to say [words] (the surviving paraphrase).
entries.punctuation: Comma before it — it comments on the main clause instead of completing it — and another comma after it when a direct quotation follows.
entries.meaning: A fossil of Elizabethan English meaning "as one might say" or "as if to say." The who is the old indefinite pronoun "anyone," a use that has otherwise died out, which is why the phrase looks ungrammatical to a modern reader rather than merely old. It survives in Shakespeare, the King James Bible, and deliberate pastiche; write as if to say in anything current.
examples: He shrugged and turned away, as who should say, "Suit yourself."
She raised an eyebrow, as who should say the matter was already settled.
The porter waved us through, as who should say our business was no business of his.
He held up the empty bottle, as who should say, "You see how it is."
They smiled at each other, as who should say they had heard that excuse before.
The old man nodded slowly, as who should say he had expected nothing else.

entries.type: subordinating (nominal relative); complementizer in indirect questions
entries.clause: nominal relative clause of manner; also an indirect question
entries.pattern: [verb] how [clause] (object of the verb). · How [clause] + [main-clause verb phrase] (the how clause is the subject). · [verb] [indirect object] how [clause]. · [verb] how to [verb phrase]. · [main clause] how [clause] (manner, = the way that).
entries.punctuation: No comma before how. It heads an integrated nominal clause, so it never takes one, in any of those positions.
entries.meaning: Covers both "in what manner" — an indirect question — and the plain "the way that" (I love how she phrases things). That second use is fully standard American English and now common in edited prose, though the way remains the more conservative choice in formal writing, where some editors still reserve how for questions.
examples: I like how you rearranged the living room.
Show me how the latch works.
How she found the address is still a mystery.
He never explained how he got the job.
Do it how you want — I don't have a preference.
It's amazing how quickly kids pick up a language.

entries.type: subordinating (manner and degree free relative) — not the conjunctive adverb
entries.clause: adverbial clause of manner or concessive condition
entries.pattern: However [clause], [main clause]. · [main clause] however [clause]. · However [adj/adv] [subject] [verb], [main clause]. · [main clause] however [adj/adv] [subject] [verb].
entries.punctuation: Comma after the fronted however clause, and nothing else — no comma when the clause trails. This is not the conjunctive adverb. The transitional however that means "but" cannot join two independent clauses with a comma; that is a comma splice (✗ We were late, however they held our table). It requires a semicolon before it and a comma after (We were late; however, they held our table), or a period and a fresh sentence. If you can swap in no matter how or in whatever way, you are looking at this subordinator and no semicolon belongs anywhere near it.
entries.meaning: Means "in whatever manner" or "to whatever degree," and it makes the main clause hold across every alternative. The movement test separates the two howevers: the conjunctive adverb slides freely around inside its own clause (They, however, held our table), while this one is locked to the front of the clause it introduces.
examples: However you slice it, the numbers don't work.
Arrange the chairs however you like.
However hard I try, I can't parallel park.
She'll finish the job however long it takes.
However the vote goes, we'll need a new budget by June.
Get here however you can.

entries.type: subordinating (compound) with a clause; prepositional with a noun phrase
entries.clause: adverbial clause of manner and comparison
entries.pattern: [main clause] in the same manner as [noun phrase]. · [main clause] in the same manner as [clause]. · In the same manner as [noun phrase], [main clause]. · [main clause] in the same manner that [clause]. · [main clause] in like manner (the clipped adverb).
entries.punctuation: Comma after the fronted phrase; no comma when it trails.
entries.meaning: The procedural register of in the same way that — the phrasing of manuals, statutes, and lab protocols, where manner is the term of art for how a step is carried out. It is the heaviest way to say this, so it earns its place only where the method itself is what is being prescribed or described. Anywhere else, the same way or just as does the identical work in half the words.
examples: Renewals are processed in the same manner as new applications.
Cut the second board in the same manner as the first.
In the same manner as the federal statute, the state law exempts family farms.
Interest accrues in the same manner as it does on an ordinary savings account.
The samples were prepared in the same manner as those in the 2019 trial.
Members are elected in the same manner that officers are.

entries.type: subordinating (compound)
entries.clause: adverbial clause of manner and comparison
entries.pattern: [main clause] in the same way that [clause]. · [main clause] in the same way [clause] (that dropped). · In the same way that [clause], [main clause]. · [main clause] in the same way as [noun phrase].
entries.punctuation: Comma after the fronted clause; no comma when it follows the main clause.
variants: in much the same way that
entries.meaning: Spells an analogy out at full length — the explicit, unambiguous version of like or just as, and the safest choice in formal writing where like would draw objections. It is heavy, so it earns its place only when the analogy is the point of the sentence; otherwise just as or the way does the same work in half the words.
examples: A good index works in the same way that a map does.
In the same way that muscles need rest, attention needs breaks.
The tax credit phases out in the same way that the old one did.
She coaches in the same way she was coached.
In the same way that no two fingerprints match, no two rooms sound alike on tape.

entries.type: subordinating (informal) with a clause; prepositional with a noun phrase
entries.clause: adverbial clause of manner and comparison
entries.pattern: [main clause] just like [noun phrase] (prepositional). · [main clause] just like [clause] (informal). · Just like [noun phrase], [main clause]. · Just like [clause], [main clause] (informal).
entries.punctuation: No comma before just like. Comma after a fronted just like phrase or clause.
entries.meaning: The everyday intensified comparison. Followed by a noun phrase (just like her mother) it is unremarkable in any register; followed by a full clause (just like I told you) it is conversational, and edited prose substitutes just as. Note that it points at resemblance, not identity — just like the original means indistinguishable from it, not the same object.
examples: She laughs just like her mother.
It went just like I told you it would.
Just like last year, the parade started twenty minutes late.
The knockoff looks just like the real thing.
He handled the interview just like a pro.
It tastes just like the version they used to sell.

entries.type: subordinating (informal) before a clause; preposition before a noun phrase; and outside the conjunction system a verb (I like it), a noun (the likes of), a suffix (businesslike), and — in speech only — a quotative (she was like, no) and a filler
entries.register: informal as a conjunction; neutral as a preposition
entries.clause: adverbial clause of manner and comparison
entries.pattern: [main clause] like [noun phrase] (prepositional; standard everywhere). · [main clause] like [clause] (manner, = as; informal). · [look/sound/seem/feel] like [clause] (= as if; informal). · Like [clause], [main clause] (fronted comment: Like I said, …). · Like [noun phrase], [main clause].
entries.punctuation: No comma before like in a comparison. Comma after a fronted like clause or phrase. A comma before it appears only when the like phrase is a supplementary aside tacked on to the end of the sentence.
entries.meaning: Like before a noun phrase — She sings like her father — has never been controversial. Like before a full clause with its own verb — She sings like her father did, It looks like it's going to rain — is what draws objections, and it is one of the longest-running arguments in American usage. On the like / as question, the facts are these. Clause-introducing like is universal in speech, standard in journalism and fiction, and still corrected in academic and formal business writing. When you need it to pass anywhere, substitute as for the manner sense (as her father did) and as if or as though for the appearance sense (as if it's going to rain). The substitution does not run the other way: with a bare noun phrase, as changes the meaning, because She works like her father compares her to him while She works as her father would mean in the role of her father.
examples: He drives like his grandfather taught him.
It looks like we're going to need a bigger table.
Nobody makes chili like my uncle does.
She writes like she talks.
The engine sounds like something's loose.
Like I said, the store opens at ten.

entries.type: subordinating (compound; archaic), usually correlative with a resumptive so
entries.clause: adverbial clause of manner and comparison, answered by so in the second half
entries.pattern: Like as [clause], so [clause]. · Like as [noun phrase], so [clause]. · [main clause] like as [clause] (dialectal).
entries.punctuation: Comma at the seam before the resumptive so, exactly as in as … so. Comma after the fronted clause when there is no so to answer it.
entries.meaning: The King James Bible's way of opening a simile: Like as a father pitieth his children, so the LORD pitieth them that fear him. Both halves are needed — like as paints the picture and so applies it — which makes it a doubled-up cousin of as … so rather than a plain manner clause. It is wholly archaic in American English outside scripture, hymnody, and pastiche, and modern translations of those same verses print As or Just as.
examples: Like as a father pitieth his children, so the Lord pitieth them that fear him.
Like as the waves make toward the pebbled shore, so do our minutes hasten to their end.
Like as a garden left untended runs to weed, so a language left unspoken thins out.
Like as a lamp burns lower toward morning, so the talk died down.
Like as the seasons turn, so the old quarrels come back around.
Like as we were taught, so we taught our own children.

entries.type: subordinating
entries.clause: adverbial clause of manner and comparison; adverbial clause of concession when fronted
entries.pattern: Much as [clause], [main clause] (concessive). · [main clause] much as [clause] (comparative). · [main clause] much as [noun phrase] [auxiliary] (elliptical: much as a cold does). · [main clause] much like [noun phrase] (the prepositional twin).
entries.punctuation: Comma after the fronted concessive clause. No comma when the comparison clause follows the main clause.
entries.meaning: Two readings split by position. Fronted, it is concessive: Much as I admire him means "although I greatly admire him." Following the main clause, it is comparative: "in much the same way that." Both sit a register above as much as and just like, which is why much as shows up in editorials and rarely in conversation.
examples: Much as I admire her work, I wouldn't want her job.
The market corrected in 2019 much as it had a decade earlier.
Much as we'd love to stay, we have an early flight.
He runs the shop much as his father did.
Much as it pains me to say it, they were right.
The rumor spread much as a cold does in a kindergarten.

entries.type: adverbial phrase (Latin) of qualified analogy — a manner adverbial in the predicate, a sentence adverbial when set off; never a clause-taking conjunction
entries.register: formal; Latin — contract, treaty, and statutory boilerplate, and academic argument
entries.clause: adverbial phrase of manner and comparison, carrying an earlier rule or argument over to a new case
entries.pattern: [provision] shall apply mutatis mutandis to [noun phrase]. · [main clause], mutatis mutandis. · Mutatis mutandis, [main clause]. · [main clause], mutatis mutandis, [continuation]. · [main clause] mutatis mutandis (bare, trailing).
entries.punctuation: No commas in the fixed drafting formula, where it is integral to the predicate: Article 12 applies mutatis mutandis to any renewal term. Comma before it when it trails as a supplement (the same holds for the city's ordinance, mutatis mutandis), comma after it when it is fronted, commas on both sides when it interrupts. Roman type in legal drafting; academic style often italicizes it. It never inflects — both words end in -is, and there is no singular.
entries.meaning: Latin for "with those things changed that need to be changed": it imports a rule or an argument whole into a second case while conceding that the names, dates, and parties will differ. An American meets it in contracts, treaties, and statutes, where it saves a drafter from setting out the same clause twice, and in academic writing, where it saves an argument from being rehearsed twice — it is boilerplate rather than prose, and outside those settings with the necessary changes says the same thing to a reader who has not studied law. Its near neighbor a fortiori moves an argument to a stronger case; this one moves it sideways to a parallel one.
examples: The provisions of Article 12 shall apply mutatis mutandis to any renewal term.
The indemnity in Section 8 applies, mutatis mutandis, to the Purchaser's affiliates.
What the court said about the county's ordinance holds, mutatis mutandis, for the city's.
Mutatis mutandis, the same objection can be raised against the second version of the argument.
The parties agree that the arbitration rules shall govern any appeal mutatis mutandis.
His account of the nineteenth-century railroads applies mutatis mutandis to broadband today.

entries.type: hedged comparison marker — prepositional before a noun phrase, subordinating (informal) before a clause
entries.clause: adverbial clause of manner and comparison, hedged
entries.pattern: [X] is sort of like [noun phrase]. · [main clause] sort of like [clause] (informal). · It's sort of like [-ing]. · Sort of like [noun phrase], [main clause]. · [X] is kind of like [noun phrase].
entries.punctuation: No comma before it. Comma after a fronted sort of like phrase. Never hyphenate it in this use: sort of like, not ✗ sort-of-like.
entries.meaning: Like with the confidence turned down: it offers a comparison and concedes in the same breath that it is approximate, which is why speakers reach for it when explaining something unfamiliar. It belongs to conversation and to writing that imitates conversation; edited prose either drops the hedge (It is like a…) or spells it out (roughly comparable to). Kind of like is the same move in a different key, and both reduce in speech to sorta and kinda.
examples: A mandolin is sort of like a violin you strum.
The new job is kind of like the old one, only with more meetings.
It felt sort of like being back in high school.
Renting there is sort of like paying a mortgage on somebody else's house.
He talks kind of like his brother does, all questions and no answers.
Sort of like the last outage, this one started with a bad update.

entries.type: subordinating (compound; nominal relative)
entries.clause: adverbial clause of manner
entries.pattern: [main clause] the way [clause]. · [main clause] the way that [clause]. · [verb] the way [clause] (object of like, hate, remember: I hate the way he says it). · The way [clause], [main clause] (idiomatic — "given that," "by his account"). · [main clause] the way in which [clause] (formal).
entries.punctuation: No comma before the way when it follows the main clause. Comma after it when the clause is fronted: The way he tells it, he saved the company.
entries.meaning: The everyday manner subordinator, and the word that solves the like-versus-as problem: it is standard in every register, takes a full clause without complaint, and never sounds stiff. Note the idiomatic fronted use, where The way he tells it means "according to his account" and The way prices are climbing means "given that."
examples: Do it the way I showed you.
The way he tells it, he practically saved the company.
I didn't like the way she said that.
The house is exactly the way we left it.
She organizes her notes the way a lawyer builds a case.
The way prices are climbing, we should book the flights now.

entries.type: fixed stance formula built on the manner subordinator the way; functions as a sentence adverbial
entries.clause: fronted adverbial clause of manner, commenting on the whole sentence
entries.pattern: The way I see it, [main clause]. · The way I see it, [clause], and [clause]. · [main clause], the way I see it. · As far as I'm concerned, [main clause] (the equivalent formula).
entries.punctuation: Comma after it, always — it is a supplement, not part of the clause it introduces. Comma before it when it trails as an afterthought.
variants: the way I look at it
entries.meaning: The everyday way of labeling an opinion as an opinion: literally "in the manner in which I see it," frozen into a discourse formula that softens a claim by owning it. It is the idiomatic fronted use of the way, and it belongs to speech, columns, and email rather than to reports. As far as I'm concerned is the same move with an edge — it marks the speaker's view as settled for their own purposes, which is why it so often introduces a refusal.
examples: The way I see it, we either raise the price or cut the hours.
The way I see it, nobody in that meeting had read the contract.
As far as I'm concerned, the matter is closed.
The way I look at it, a used car with service records beats a new one without.
She's already apologized, the way I see it, and that should be the end of it.
As far as I'm concerned, they can keep the deposit — I'm not going back.

entries.type: subordinating (compound)
entries.clause: adverbial clause of proportion and correspondence
entries.pattern: [main clause] according as [clause]. · According as [clause], [main clause]. · [main clause] according as [clause] or [clause] (the paired-outcome form). · [main clause] according to whether [clause] (the modern paraphrase). · [main clause] according to [noun phrase] (prepositional — a different word class).
entries.punctuation: Comma after the fronted clause; no comma when it follows the main clause. No comma before the internal or that pairs the two outcomes.
entries.meaning: Means "in proportion to whether" or "depending on which of these turns out to be true" — the outcome varies with the condition. It survives in legal, mathematical, and older literary prose. Note that it is a conjunction taking a clause, unlike the everyday preposition according to, which takes a noun phrase; everyday American English says depending on whether instead.
examples: The rate rises or falls according as the index moves.
According as the weather allows, the ceremony will be held outdoors or in the hall.
Each parcel is taxed according as it is classified residential or commercial.
The sign of the result changes according as n is even or odd.
They will be judged according as they have acted.

entries.type: conjunctive adverb of correspondence; also an ordinary degree adverb inside the clause (a correspondingly larger bill)
entries.register: neutral to formal; reporting, policy, and technical prose
entries.clause: sentence adverbial saying its clause moves in step with the one before it; degree modifier in the adjectival use
entries.pattern: [Independent clause]; correspondingly, [independent clause]. · [Independent clause]. Correspondingly, [independent clause]. · [main clause], and [subject] [verb phrase] correspondingly. · [subject], correspondingly, [verb phrase]. · [main clause] a correspondingly [comparative adjective] [noun] (degree use).
entries.punctuation: Comma after it when it opens a clause; commas on both sides when it interrupts a subject and its verb. Between two independent clauses it needs a semicolon or a period in front of it — a comma there is a splice: ✗ The levy rose, correspondingly receipts fell. ✓ The levy rose; correspondingly, receipts fell. No comma at all in the degree use, where it simply modifies an adjective: a correspondingly smaller refund.
entries.meaning: The adverb of matched movement: whatever the first clause reports going up or down, the second clause is said to follow it. That makes it narrower than similarly, which claims only a resemblance — correspondingly claims a linkage between two quantities, and it rings false when nothing is actually varying. Its clause-taking equivalents are in proportion as and the more … the more, which say the same thing with a subordinator instead of an adverb, and a comma instead of a semicolon.
examples: The district enrolled two hundred more students; correspondingly, it hired six more teachers.
Freight volumes fell all spring. Correspondingly, rail revenue came in under forecast.
Premiums went up nine percent, and coverage narrowed correspondingly.
As the deductible rises, the monthly payment drops correspondingly.
The new building is twice the size of the old one and carries a correspondingly larger tax bill.
Testing slowed over the holiday; correspondingly, the reported case counts dipped and then caught up.

entries.type: subordinating (compound); the shortened in proportion to is a preposition taking a noun phrase
entries.clause: adverbial clause of proportion and correspondence
entries.pattern: [main clause] in proportion as [clause]. · In proportion as [clause], [main clause]. · [main clause] in proportion to [noun phrase] (prepositional — a different word class). · In proportion as [clause], so [clause] (with a resumptive so opening the second half).
entries.punctuation: Comma after the clause when it is fronted; no comma when it follows the main clause. Nothing inside the clause takes one.
entries.meaning: Says that two quantities move together — as one rises or falls, so does the other. It is the clause-taking twin of the everyday preposition in proportion to, and the difference is only what follows: the conjunction takes a full clause (in proportion as the debt grows), the preposition takes a noun phrase (in proportion to the debt). In American English the conjunction is confined to formal argument, older prose, mathematics, and physical law; ordinary writing reaches for the more … the more or as … so, which say the same thing and sound like this century.
examples: Wages rose in proportion as the cost of housing climbed.
In proportion as the light fades, the colors go flat.
A tax is fair in proportion as it tracks the ability to pay.
The pressure increases in proportion as the volume shrinks.
In proportion as the town grew, the old rivalries lost their heat.
He grew more careful in proportion as the stakes rose.
In proportion as the population aged, so the tax base narrowed.

entries.type: adverb of one-to-one correspondence — not a conjunction; it distributes the members of one list across the members of another and joins nothing
entries.register: neutral to formal; statistical, scientific, and journalistic
entries.clause: adverbial of correspondence, almost always clause-final
entries.pattern: [list A] [verb] [list B], respectively. · [X] and [Y] were [A] and [B], respectively. · [X], [Y], and [Z] [verb] [A], [B], and [C], respectively. · [main clause] ([A] and [B], respectively). · [X] and [Y], respectively, [verb phrase].
entries.punctuation: A comma before it at the end of the clause, which is where it almost always sits; commas on both sides in the rarer medial position. Because it is an adverb with no linking function at all, it can never stand between two independent clauses in any punctuation — not with a comma and not with a semicolon. Do not spell it respectfully, which means "with respect" and is a different word.
entries.meaning: Pairs off two lists in sequence: Chicago and Denver grew four and seven percent, respectively assigns four to Chicago and seven to Denver. It only works when both lists have the same number of members in the same order, and it is empty when there is only one item on a side (✗ Sales rose in Ohio, respectively). It is catalogued here as the last member of the correspondence family and as a warning: writers reach for it as though it meant in turn, accordingly, or each in its own way, and it means none of those.
examples: The two bills cleared the House and the Senate by margins of twelve and three votes, respectively.
Chicago and Denver grew four and seven percent, respectively, over the decade.
Gold, silver, and bronze went to Norway, Japan, and Canada, respectively.
The control and treatment groups reported 14 and 31 adverse events, respectively.
Her first and second novels sold nine hundred and ninety thousand copies, respectively.
The north and south wings were built in 1904 and 1927, respectively.

entries.type: correlative (proportional comparative)
entries.clause: paired comparative clauses — the first is subordinate, the second is the main clause
entries.pattern: The [comparative], the [comparative]. · The more [clause], the more [clause]. · The [comparative] [noun], the [comparative] [noun] (verbless).
entries.punctuation: Comma at the seam between the two halves — required in edited prose and the single rule learners most often miss. No comma inside either half. Very short verbless pairs are sometimes printed without it, but The sooner, the better is the standard form.
entries.meaning: Says that two quantities rise or fall together. The the here is not the article but a surviving Old English instrumental form meaning "by that much," which is why it can stand in front of a comparative and why both halves need one. Word order is fixed: the comparative phrase moves to the front of each clause, so it is The more he explained, never He explained the more.
examples: The more he explained, the less I understood.
The sooner you file, the sooner you get the refund.
The colder it gets, the more the pipes rattle.
The harder she practiced, the better she played.
The bigger the crowd, the longer the wait.
The sooner, the better.

entries.type: preposition (complex) — it takes a noun phrase or a nominal wh- clause, never a finite clause; the clause-taking form is the conjunction according as
entries.clause: prepositional phrase of source, standard, or correspondence; supplementary when fronted
entries.pattern: According to [noun phrase], [main clause] (attribution). · [main clause], according to [noun phrase] (attribution, trailing). · [main clause] according to [noun phrase] (standard or correspondence). · [main clause] according to whether [clause]. · [main clause] according to [wh-clause].
entries.punctuation: Comma after the fronted phrase, always. In the attribution sense a trailing phrase takes a comma before it (The flight is on time, according to the airline); in the correspondence sense a trailing phrase is integral to the predicate and takes none (Seats were assigned according to rank).
entries.meaning: Two jobs share one phrase. In the attribution sense it names whose account you are relaying (according to the police), and it carries a faint note of distance — you are reporting the claim, not vouching for it, which is why According to me sounds wrong and in my opinion is the phrase for your own view. In the correspondence sense it names the standard something varies with (paid according to experience), and that is the sense whose clause-taking twin is according as.
examples: According to the airline, the delay is weather.
Seats were assigned according to seniority.
The bill will be scored according to the committee's own formula.
According to the label, the paint needs two hours between coats.
Attendance rose and fell according to the weather.
The fee changes according to whether you file online or by mail.
It rained all weekend in the mountains, according to my sister.

entries.type: phrasal comparison marker — prepositional with as before a noun phrase; a conjunctive adverb when it stands alone
entries.clause: supplementary comparative phrase of resemblance; adverbial in the bare form
entries.pattern: [main clause] along the same lines as [noun phrase]. · Along the same lines, [main clause] (adverbial). · [main clause] along the same lines (bare, trailing). · [main clause] along much the same lines as [noun phrase]. · [Independent clause]; along the same lines, [independent clause].
entries.punctuation: No comma before along the same lines as when it completes the comparison. Comma after the bare form when it opens a sentence. Standing between two independent clauses it is an adverb and needs a semicolon or a period in front of it — a comma there is a splice.
entries.meaning: Says that the second thing follows the pattern of the first without matching it exactly — the register of memos, workshops, and editorial notes, where it turns a suggestion into a direction. With as it names the model it is following; bare, it points back at whatever was just said. Its neighbor in the same vein covers tone and style, while this one covers approach and design.
examples: The second proposal runs along the same lines as the first, with a smaller budget.
Along the same lines, the committee wants a shorter application form.
We're thinking along the same lines — let's compare notes.
She wants a mural along the same lines as the one in the lobby.
The state bill was drafted along much the same lines as the federal one.
The two reports reach different numbers, but they argue along the same lines.

entries.type: phrasal comparison marker (prepositional) — it takes a noun phrase, most often a figure, never a finite clause
entries.register: formal; the register of reporting and statistics
entries.clause: supplementary comparative phrase naming the figure or the case being set against
entries.pattern: [figure] as against [figure]. · [main clause], as against [noun phrase]. · As against [noun phrase], [main clause]. · [X], as against [Y], [verb phrase].
entries.punctuation: No comma in the tight figure-against-figure pair (eleven percent as against nine). Comma before it when it trails as a supplement, comma after it when it is fronted, commas on both sides when it interrupts a subject and its verb.
entries.meaning: The statistician's contrast: it sets one measured value beside another and lets the gap speak for itself. British writing also uses it freely in the as opposed to sense, but American English mostly keeps it for numbers and reaches for as opposed to or versus everywhere else. Whatever follows has to be the same kind of quantity as what precedes it, or the comparison means nothing.
examples: Turnout was thirty-one percent, as against nineteen in the last off-year election.
The county recorded 412 permits, as against 380 a year earlier.
As against the projected shortfall, the actual gap was small.
He was sentenced to two years, as against the ten the statute allows.
Revenue grew four percent, as against an industry average of one.
As against what the district spends per student, the neighboring county looks generous.

entries.type: phrasal comparison marker (reduced participial phrase, functioning as a preposition) — it takes a noun phrase or a nominal wh- clause, never an ordinary finite clause
entries.clause: reduced adverbial clause of comparison, supplementary
entries.pattern: [main clause], as compared with [noun phrase]. · As compared with [noun phrase], [main clause]. · [X], as compared with [Y], [verb phrase]. · [main clause], as compared with [wh-clause].
entries.punctuation: Set off with commas — comma after it when fronted, comma before it when it trails. It is a supplement, not an integral part of the clause.
entries.meaning: The report-and-abstract way of naming the baseline of a comparison. Traditionally compared with measures like against like on one scale (two quarters, two cities) and compared to likens unlike things; in current American usage the two have largely merged, but with remains the safer choice in technical writing. Make sure the thing being compared is the subject of the main clause, or the phrase dangles.
examples: Emissions fell four percent, as compared with the same quarter last year.
As compared with the pilot program, the statewide rollout cost twice as much.
Response times improved, as compared with the baseline measured in March.
The new alloy is brittle, as compared with standard steel.
As compared with her earlier novels, this one is almost cheerful.
Enrollment is up nine percent, as compared with what the district projected in the spring.

entries.type: phrasal comparison marker (adjectival preposition) — it takes a noun phrase or an -ing form, never a finite clause
entries.clause: supplementary comparative phrase drawing a line between two categories
entries.pattern: [X], as distinct from [Y], [verb phrase]. · [main clause], as distinct from [noun phrase]. · As distinct from [noun phrase], [main clause]. · [main clause] as distinct from [-ing].
entries.punctuation: Commas on both sides when it interrupts a subject and its verb; comma before it when it trails as a supplement; comma after it when fronted. No comma inside a tight paired phrase (advice as distinct from instruction).
entries.meaning: Draws a categorical line rather than stating a preference: it says the two things differ in kind, and it assumes the reader might have run them together. That is what separates it from as opposed to, which names an alternative that was rejected — as distinct from rejects nothing, it only sorts. Keep the two halves the same kind of phrase, and make the second one the thing the reader was likelier to have meant.
examples: The report covers full-time staff, as distinct from contractors.
What she offered was advice, as distinct from an instruction.
As distinct from the state tax, the city levy applies only to earned income.
He studies climate, as distinct from weather, and the difference matters to his funding.
The lease covers repairs, as distinct from improvements the tenant chooses to make.
We're counting how many people read the email, as distinct from how many opened it.

entries.type: phrasal comparison marker (participial preposition) — it takes a noun phrase or an -ing form, never a finite clause
entries.clause: supplementary comparative phrase drawing a technical distinction
entries.pattern: [X], as distinguished from [Y], [verb phrase]. · [main clause], as distinguished from [noun phrase]. · As distinguished from [noun phrase], [main clause]. · [main clause] as distinguished from [-ing].
entries.punctuation: Commas on both sides when it interrupts a subject and its verb; comma before it when it trails; comma after it when fronted.
entries.meaning: The courtroom's version of as distinct from, and a shade more deliberate: distinguished implies that somebody has drawn the line on purpose, which is exactly what a judge does in distinguishing one case from another. Reserve it for genuinely technical distinctions in formal prose, where the line being drawn carries consequences. Everywhere else it is three syllables of ceremony that as distinct from supplies for free.
examples: The statute reaches negligence, as distinguished from deliberate harm.
Ordinary income, as distinguished from capital gains, is taxed at the full rate.
As distinguished from the earlier ruling, this opinion turns on intent.
She was hired as an employee, as distinguished from an independent contractor.
The term refers to the printed record, as distinguished from the recording of the hearing.
Fair use, as distinguished from a negotiated license, requires no permission at all.

entries.type: fixed topic-shifting marker — prepositional in effect, taking a noun phrase, a pronoun, an -ing form, or a nominal wh- clause, never a finite clause of its own
entries.clause: fronted adverbial phrase of respect, naming the topic the main clause is about to settle
entries.pattern: As for [noun phrase], [main clause]. · As for [pronoun], [main clause]. · As for [-ing], [main clause]. · As for [wh-clause], [main clause]. · As for the rest / as for that, [main clause].
entries.punctuation: Comma after the phrase, always — it is a fronted supplement, not part of the clause that follows. Unlike when it comes to, it does not trail the main clause, so the trailing comma question never arises: write As for the budget, we'll take that up in September, not ✗ We'll take that up in September as for the budget.
entries.meaning: Hands the sentence over to a new topic — usually one the reader has been waiting for — by picking something up and saying "now that one." That is what separates it from when it comes to, which narrows a general claim to one domain instead of switching subjects, and it is why as for so often carries a faint note of dismissal: As for the neighbors, they can think what they like. It takes a phrase and never a clause, so write as for whether the road reopens, not ✗ as for the road reopens.
examples: As for the budget, we'll take that up in September.
The kids loved the museum. As for me, I loved the café.
As for whether the road reopens by Friday, nobody at the county will say.
He's agreed to the price. As for the closing date, that's still open.
As for getting there early, don't bother — the doors don't open until seven.
The engine is sound. As for the transmission, I'd get a second opinion.

entries.type: reduced comparison marker — the manner subordinator as with an elliptical clause, prepositional in effect
entries.register: neutral; the clarifier use is informal
entries.clause: reduced adverbial clause of comparison; also an exemplifying phrase
entries.pattern: [main clause], as in [noun phrase] (parallel case). · [main clause] as in [noun phrase] (integral). · [sound / sense], as in "[example]" (illustration). · As in [noun phrase], [main clause]. · [statement] — as in, [restatement] (spoken clarifier).
entries.punctuation: Comma before it when it adds a supplementary parallel or an illustration (a soft g, as in "giraffe"). No comma when it is integral to the predicate (The vowel is long as in "make"). Comma after it when fronted, and a comma after it in the spoken clarifier use.
entries.meaning: A compression of as it is in: it points at another case where the same thing holds, and in its commonest use it names the example that pins down a pronunciation or a sense. Speech has stretched it into a clarifier — We need it soon, as in today — where it introduces a restatement rather than a comparison, and that use stays out of formal writing. Whatever follows is a noun phrase, so it never takes a clause of its own.
examples: The vowel is short, as in "bet."
Federal aid arrived late, as in every previous flood.
As in the pilot program, the classes are capped at fifteen.
It's a soft g, as in "giraffe."
Turnout collapsed in the suburbs, as in 2018.
She wants it done soon — as in, before the board meets.

entries.type: phrasal comparison marker (participial preposition) — it takes a noun phrase, an -ing form, or a nominal wh- clause, never a finite clause of its own
entries.clause: supplementary comparative phrase naming the rejected alternative
entries.pattern: [main clause] as opposed to [noun phrase]. · [main clause] as opposed to [-ing]. · As opposed to [noun phrase], [main clause]. · [X], as opposed to [Y], [verb phrase]. · [main clause] as opposed to [wh-clause].
entries.punctuation: Comma after the fronted phrase. A comma before it when it trails as a supplement (The grant is a subsidy, as opposed to a loan); none when the two halves are a tight pair inside the clause (leasing as opposed to buying). Commas on both sides when it interrupts subject and verb.
entries.meaning: Names the alternative that was not chosen, and presses on the distinction harder than rather than does — it is the phrase you reach for when you expect the reader to have confused the two things. Being a preposition, it takes a noun phrase, an -ing form, or a noun clause, never a bare infinitive: as opposed to renting, not as opposed to rent, whenever the other half of the pair is a gerund. Keep the two halves the same shape and it never goes wrong.
examples: The grant is a subsidy, as opposed to a loan the city expects back.
As opposed to last year's format, this conference runs three days.
She was hired as a consultant, as opposed to a full-time employee.
We're talking about the printed edition, as opposed to whatever is on the website.
They're leasing this time as opposed to buying.
The tax applies to income, as opposed to assets.

entries.type: reduced comparison marker — the manner subordinator as with an elliptical clause; prepositional in effect, taking a noun phrase or an -ing form
entries.clause: reduced adverbial clause of comparison, supplementary
entries.pattern: As with [noun phrase], [main clause]. · [main clause], as with [noun phrase]. · As with [-ing], [main clause]. · As with [noun phrase], so with [noun phrase] (the balanced pair).
entries.punctuation: Comma after the fronted phrase, always. Comma before it when it trails, because it comments on the whole clause instead of completing it.
entries.meaning: Short for as is the case with: it names a parallel case and claims that the main clause runs the same way there. It is the workhorse opener of explanatory prose — As with most rules, there are exceptions — because it lets a writer generalize and qualify in three words. Watch for the dangler: whatever follows as with has to be genuinely comparable to the subject of the main clause.
examples: As with most rules, there are exceptions.
As with the first dose, the second one left her arm sore for a day.
The fee is waived for students, as with the museum's other programs.
As with buying a house, the closing costs are where the surprises live.
As with her earlier books, the plot matters less than the voice.
Snow closed the pass again, as with every storm this winter.

entries.type: phrasal comparison marker (prepositional) — it takes a noun phrase, never a finite clause
entries.clause: adverbial phrase naming the model a claim or a coinage is reasoned from
entries.pattern: [main clause] by analogy with [noun phrase]. · By analogy with [noun phrase], [main clause]. · [X] was coined / formed / decided by analogy with [Y]. · [main clause], by analogy with [noun phrase].
