entries.punctuation: Comma after the fronted phrase. No comma when it trails as part of the predicate (coined by analogy with "workaholic"); a comma before it only when it is a genuine aside.
entries.meaning: Names the case a conclusion was reasoned from, not merely a case it is being measured against — which is what separates it from compared to. Linguists use it for the process that gives us chocoholic out of alcoholic; lawyers use it for reasoning from a decided case to an undecided one. In American technical prose prefer with; by analogy to is common but reads a shade looser.
examples: The word was coined by analogy with "workaholic."
By analogy with the postal rule, the court treated the email as sent on dispatch.
Early chemists named the gas by analogy with the elements they already knew.
By analogy with municipal bonds, the new instrument pays tax-free interest.
Children build past tenses by analogy with the regular verbs they know, which is why "goed" turns up before "went."
The argument runs by analogy with the flu vaccine, and it breaks down for the same reasons.

entries.type: conjunctive adverb (fixed phrase) of parallel inference
entries.clause: sentence adverbial marking its clause as following from the same reasoning that produced the last one
entries.pattern: [Independent clause]; by the same token, [independent clause]. · [Independent clause]. By the same token, [independent clause]. · [main clause], and by the same token [clause]. · [subject], by the same token, [verb phrase]. · If [clause], then by the same token [clause].
entries.punctuation: Comma after it when it opens a clause; commas on both sides when it interrupts a subject and its verb. Standing between two independent clauses it is an adverb, so it takes a semicolon or a period in front of it — a comma there is a splice: ✗ He can't vote on it, by the same token neither can she. ✓ He can't vote on it; by the same token, neither can she. Only a coordinating and can carry it across with a comma.
entries.meaning: Says that the reason just given cuts a second way as well — not that two things merely resemble each other, but that one argument covers both. That is the line between it and its neighbors: likewise and similarly point at a resemblance, while by the same token points at a shared premise, which is why it so often introduces the less welcome half of a principle. The token is the old sense "sign, evidence," not a coin.
examples: A landlord can't be forced to rent to anyone he pleases; by the same token, a tenant can't be forced to stay.
If experience should count toward the promotion, then by the same token it should count toward the pay.
She refused to comment on the lawsuit. By the same token, she wouldn't discuss the settlement talks.
Cheap money made the boom possible, and by the same token it made the crash worse.
The rule keeps outside firms from bidding; by the same token, it keeps the town from finding a cheaper contractor.
He never asked anyone for help and, by the same token, never offered any.

entries.type: phrasal comparison marker (reduced participial phrase, functioning as a preposition) — it takes a noun phrase, an -ing form, or a nominal wh- clause, never an ordinary finite clause; compare is also a plain transitive verb (He compared the two drafts)
entries.clause: reduced adverbial clause of comparison
entries.pattern: Compared to [noun phrase], [main clause]. · [main clause] compared to [noun phrase]. · [main clause] compared to [wh-clause]. · [main clause] compared to [-ing]. · [X], compared to [Y], [verb phrase].
entries.punctuation: Comma after the fronted phrase, always. When it trails the main clause the comma is optional and usually dropped if the phrase is short and integral (The repair was cheap compared to replacing the whole unit); keep it when the phrase is a genuine afterthought. Commas on both sides when it interrupts subject and verb.
entries.meaning: The everyday version of the same move, and the one American speakers actually use. Classically compared to likens two unlike things to make a point (He compared the city to an anthill) while compared with sets two like things side by side, but as a sentence-opening adverbial compared to now covers both. The fronted form must still describe the subject: Compared to last winter, this one has been mild works because both are winters.
examples: Compared to last winter, this one has been mild.
The rent is reasonable compared to what friends pay downtown.
Compared to the original, the remake feels rushed.
Two hours is nothing compared to the drive we made last summer.
Compared to most of his classmates, he reads several grades ahead.
The repair was cheap compared to replacing the whole unit.

entries.type: adjective + preposition; a phrasal marker of conformity, and a supplementary adverbial when fronted
entries.register: neutral to formal; heavily used in science, medicine, and law
entries.clause: predicative complement after be; adverbial phrase of conformity when fronted or set off
entries.pattern: [X] is consistent with [noun phrase]. · Consistent with [noun phrase], [main clause]. · [main clause], consistent with [noun phrase]. · [X], consistent with [Y], [verb phrase]. · [X] is consistent with [wh-clause].
entries.punctuation: No comma in the predicative use (The results are consistent with the model). Comma after the fronted adverbial (Consistent with earlier work, the trial found no effect), and a comma before it when it trails as a supplement.
entries.meaning: Says that two things fit together without contradiction — and note how much weaker that is than saying they match. In scientific and medical writing it is a deliberate hedge: findings consistent with pneumonia means the picture fits pneumonia, not that pneumonia is proved, and the double negative not inconsistent with hedges further still. Fronted, it becomes a conformity adverbial that ties a new result to an established one.
examples: The blood work is consistent with a viral infection.
Consistent with earlier studies, the trial found no effect on mortality.
His account is consistent with what the neighbors told police.
The city's decision is consistent with the zoning code, whatever the neighbors think.
Consistent with the new policy, all requests now go through the portal.
The wear on the tire is consistent with driving on it flat.

entries.type: phrasal comparison marker (prepositional) — it takes a noun phrase or an -ing form, never a finite clause; the clipped by comparison and in comparison are conjunctive adverbs
entries.clause: reduced adverbial clause of comparison, supplementary
entries.pattern: In comparison with [noun phrase], [main clause]. · [main clause] in comparison with [noun phrase]. · [X], in comparison with [Y], [verb phrase]. · [main clause] in comparison with [-ing]. · [Independent clause]; by comparison, [independent clause] (the clipped adverb).
entries.punctuation: Comma after the fronted phrase; comma before it when it trails and is supplementary. The clipped forms punctuate differently, because they are adverbs and not prepositions: between two independent clauses by comparison needs a semicolon or a period before it (The first draft was long; by comparison, the second is a pamphlet), and a comma there is a splice.
entries.meaning: The heaviest member of the family, at home in reports and academic prose. It says exactly what compared with says in three more words, so prefer the shorter form unless the sentence already has a compared doing other work. The clipped by comparison can stand alone after a full clause, which the long form cannot.
examples: In comparison with its neighbors, the state spends very little per student.
The delay was trivial in comparison with the problems that followed.
In comparison with the 1990s, violent crime is down sharply.
Her early paintings look tentative in comparison with the later work.
The second proposal is modest in comparison with the first.
The first draft ran three hundred pages; by comparison, the second is a pamphlet. (the clipped form is an adverb — semicolon, not comma)

entries.type: phrasal marker of conformity (prepositional) — it takes a noun phrase, never a finite clause
entries.clause: adverbial phrase of conformity; supplementary when fronted
entries.pattern: [main clause] in conformity with [noun phrase]. · In conformity with [noun phrase], [main clause]. · [X] is in conformity with [Y]. · [main clause], in conformity with [noun phrase].
entries.punctuation: Comma after the fronted phrase. No comma when it trails as part of the predicate; a comma before it only when it is a genuine aside.
entries.meaning: The rule-book register: it says the thing described has been measured against a stated standard and does not depart from it. In accordance with is its everyday twin and reads better in most sentences, while in compliance with is the one to use when the standard is mandatory and somebody could be penalized for missing it. Keep it for documents that actually name the standard being met; anywhere else it is bureaucratic padding for under or following.
examples: The audit was conducted in conformity with generally accepted accounting principles.
In conformity with the treaty, both governments filed annual reports.
The building was inspected and found to be in conformity with the fire code.
Ballots are counted in conformity with procedures published before the election.
In conformity with long practice, the chair recognized the minority leader first.
The device is manufactured in conformity with the European standard as well as the American one.

entries.type: phrasal comparison marker (prepositional) — it takes a noun phrase, an -ing form, or a nominal wh- clause, never a finite clause; strip the to and bare in contrast is a conjunctive adverb
entries.clause: supplementary comparative phrase of contrast
entries.pattern: In contrast to [noun phrase], [main clause]. · [main clause], in contrast to [noun phrase]. · [X], in contrast to [Y], [verb phrase]. · In contrast to [-ing], [main clause]. · [main clause], in contrast to [wh-clause]. · [Independent clause]; in contrast, [independent clause] (the bare adverb).
entries.punctuation: Comma after the fronted phrase, always. Comma before it when it trails, because it comments on the main clause rather than completing it; the comma disappears only in the tight predicate use (small in contrast to the effort), which is rarer here than with compared to. Commas on both sides when it interrupts a subject and its verb. The stripped-down in contrast is where writers go wrong: it is an adverb, so between two independent clauses it needs a semicolon or a period, never a comma. ✗ Rural counties shrank, in contrast the suburbs grew. ✓ Rural counties shrank; in contrast, the suburbs grew.
variants: in sharp / stark / marked contrast to
entries.meaning: Names the thing the subject differs from, and unlike the compare family it is only ever about difference — there is no reading in which it finds two things alike. Its nearest neighbors split the work three ways: unlike says the same thing in one word and takes the same commas, as opposed to points at a rejected alternative rather than a plain difference, and whereas does the job with a full clause instead of a phrase. Because the phrase has no verb of its own, whatever follows to has to be the same kind of thing as the subject of the main clause, or it dangles: ✗ In contrast to last year, the mayor added two positions compares a year to a mayor.
examples: In contrast to her sister, she never took a music lesson in her life.
The new regulation, in contrast to the old one, covers part-time workers.
Attendance held steady downtown, in contrast to the sharp drop in the suburbs.
In contrast to what the brochure promised, the room faced the parking lot.
Rents fell here, in contrast to almost every other city on the coast.
In contrast to borrowing at a fixed rate, a variable loan moves with the index.
The coasts lost residents; in contrast, the mountain states gained them. (bare adverb — semicolon, not comma)

entries.type: phrasal marker of conformity (prepositional) — it takes a noun phrase or an -ing form, never a finite clause
entries.clause: adverbial phrase of conformity and harmony; supplementary when fronted
entries.pattern: In keeping with [noun phrase], [main clause]. · [main clause] in keeping with [noun phrase]. · [X] is in keeping with [Y]. · In keeping with [-ing], [main clause]. · [X] is out of keeping with [Y] (the negative).
entries.punctuation: Comma after the fronted phrase, always. No comma when it trails as part of the predicate (a plain stone in keeping with the rest of the churchyard); comma before it when it is a supplement.
entries.meaning: Conformity with a tone, a tradition, or a style rather than with a rule — which is what separates it from in accordance with, and why it lives in obituaries, architecture criticism, and dress codes. It has a working negative, out of keeping with, that no other member of this family really offers, and that negative is where the phrase does its sharpest work. What follows it has to be something a manner could harmonize with, not a number.
examples: In keeping with family tradition, the service was small and early.
The addition uses local stone, in keeping with the older wing.
Her decision to walk away is entirely in keeping with everything she has written.
In keeping with the season, the menu is all root vegetables.
The tone of the letter was out of keeping with the rest of the file.
Guests dressed in keeping with the invitation, which had asked for "garden formal."

entries.type: phrasal marker of conformity (prepositional) — it takes a noun phrase, never a finite clause
entries.register: neutral; business, journalism, and policy writing
entries.clause: adverbial phrase of conformity and correspondence; supplementary when fronted
entries.pattern: [X] is in line with [noun phrase]. · In line with [noun phrase], [main clause]. · [main clause] in line with [noun phrase]. · [X] is broadly / roughly in line with [Y]. · bring / keep [X] in line with [Y].
entries.punctuation: Comma after the fronted phrase. No comma when it trails, in the predicative use (Rents are in line with the county) or the adverbial one alike.
entries.meaning: The quarterly-report phrase: earnings come in in line with expectations, and the whole job of the words is to say that a figure landed where it was supposed to. It also has an active use — bring state law in line with the federal statute — meaning to make one thing match another. The literal ancestor still shows through, so what follows should be something a number or a policy could be lined up against.
examples: Revenue came in in line with what analysts expected.
In line with the new guidance, the district moved its start time back an hour.
The proposal would bring state law in line with the federal statute.
Rents here are roughly in line with the rest of the county.
His testimony was out of line with everything in the written record.
In line with past practice, the committee released the transcript a week later.

entries.type: phrasal comparison marker — prepositional with as before a noun phrase; a conjunctive adverb when it stands alone
entries.clause: supplementary comparative phrase of tone and style; adverbial in the bare form
entries.pattern: [main clause] in the same vein as [noun phrase]. · In the same vein, [main clause] (adverbial). · [main clause], in the same vein (trailing). · [Independent clause]; in the same vein, [independent clause]. · In a similar vein, [main clause].
entries.punctuation: No comma before in the same vein as when it completes the comparison. Comma after the bare form when it opens a sentence. Between two independent clauses it is an adverb and takes a semicolon or a period before it, never a comma: ✗ The first essay was funny, in the same vein the second is grim.
entries.meaning: Points at a shared manner, tone, or line of thought rather than at a measurable likeness — the metaphor is a vein of ore running through rock, so what continues is a seam of the same material. Bare, it works as a transition between two remarks of the same kind; with as, it names the work or the comment it is echoing. Keep it for style and register, and use along the same lines when the resemblance is one of method.
examples: Her second collection is in the same vein as the first, only funnier.
In the same vein, the mayor proposed cutting parking fees downtown.
The sequel continues in the same vein for another four hundred pages.
He told one story about his father; in the same vein, she told one about her mother.
In a similar vein, the committee asked for a plainer summary.
The painting is in the same vein as his early work, before the murals.

entries.type: preposition (Latin) — "in the capacity of," "considered as"; it takes a bare noun phrase, never a clause
entries.clause: prepositional phrase of role and respect
entries.pattern: [noun] qua [the same or a related noun] (the novel qua novel). · [X], qua [role], [verb phrase]. · [main clause] qua [noun phrase]. · considered qua [noun phrase].
entries.punctuation: No commas around it in the tight noun-qua-noun pair — it binds to the nouns on either side. Commas only when the whole qua phrase interrupts a subject and its verb (The judge, qua judge, has no opinion). Set it in roman; it has been English long enough not to need italics.
entries.meaning: Latin for "in the capacity of," and the word philosophers use to isolate one aspect of a thing from everything else that is true about it: the novel qua novel means the novel considered purely as a novel, setting aside its politics, its sales, and its author. English as does the same job in the role sense, so qua earns its keep only where repeating the noun is the point. Used loosely for and or versus it is simply wrong — what follows qua is a role, not a second party.
examples: We are studying the building qua architecture, not qua real estate.
The judge, qua judge, has no opinion about the wisdom of the statute.
Money qua money is worthless; it matters only for what it buys.
He was writing qua historian rather than qua citizen.
The question is whether a corporation qua corporation can hold a religious belief.
Sociology treats the group qua group, not as a pile of individuals.

entries.type: phrasal comparison marker (prepositional) — it takes a noun phrase or an -ing form, never a finite clause; relative is also a plain adjective (relative humidity) and a noun (a distant relative)
entries.register: formal to neutral; technical, financial, and academic
entries.clause: adverbial phrase of comparison naming the reference point; also a phrase of topic in the "concerning" sense
entries.pattern: [main clause] relative to [noun phrase]. · Relative to [noun phrase], [main clause]. · [X] is [comparative] relative to [Y]. · [figure] relative to [figure]. · [main clause] relative to [-ing].
entries.punctuation: Comma after the fronted phrase. No comma when it trails, because it completes the measurement rather than commenting on it.
entries.meaning: Names the baseline a measurement is taken from, which makes it the phrase of choice wherever a number only means something against a reference — velocity, exchange rates, cost of living, performance against a benchmark. That is what separates it from compared to: compared to invites the reader to notice a difference, while relative to says the second term is the frame the first is being measured in. It has a looser second life meaning "concerning" (documents relative to the sale), which reads as legal boilerplate and is better written about.
examples: The dollar has weakened relative to the euro.
Relative to its population, the state sends an outsized delegation to Washington.
Housing costs are high here relative to wages.
The fund underperformed relative to its benchmark for a third straight quarter.
Relative to last quarter, complaints are down by a third.
Measure the shadow relative to the height of the pole.

entries.type: preposition of contrast — the negative of prepositional like; also an adjective in It's unlike her to be late
entries.clause: supplementary comparative phrase; it has no clause-taking form at all
entries.pattern: Unlike [noun phrase], [main clause]. · [main clause], unlike [noun phrase]. · [X], unlike [Y], [verb phrase]. · It is unlike [person] to [verb phrase] (adjective).
entries.punctuation: Comma after the fronted phrase, always. Comma before it when it trails as a supplement. Commas on both sides when it interrupts a subject and its verb: My sister, unlike me, reads the manual.
entries.meaning: The negative counterpart of prepositional like, and the one member of this family with no conjunction use whatsoever — there is no unlike he does, only unlike him. Because it is a bare phrase, it dangles easily: Unlike most cities, the streets here are numbered compares cities to streets. Whatever follows unlike has to be the same kind of thing as the subject of the main clause. It carries a second, idiomatic "out of character" sense (It's unlike her to be late), where it is an adjective rather than a preposition.
examples: Unlike her brother, she never learned to drive.
The new lease, unlike the old one, lets us sublet.
Unlike most of the coast, this stretch has no public access.
He took the criticism well, unlike the last person in the job.
It's unlike Marco to leave without saying goodbye.
Unlike the earlier models, this one runs quietly enough to sit next to.

entries.type: preposition (from French) — "in relation to," "as against"; it takes a noun phrase, never a clause, and it is also a noun meaning "counterpart"
entries.clause: adverbial phrase of relation and comparison
entries.pattern: [main clause] vis-à-vis [noun phrase]. · [X]'s position vis-à-vis [Y]. · Vis-à-vis [noun phrase], [main clause]. · [X] is [comparative] vis-à-vis [Y].
entries.punctuation: Comma after the fronted phrase; no comma when it trails. Keep both hyphens, and keep the grave accent — vis-à-vis is the dictionary spelling in American English, and the bare vis-a-vis is a common second best.
entries.meaning: Literally "face to face," and the surviving sense keeps that picture: two parties lined up opposite each other, with one measured against the other. Analysts and diplomats use it for standing and leverage — the union's position vis-à-vis management — where compared to would sound merely arithmetical. In loose American usage it has drifted toward a vague "regarding," and that drift draws complaints; keep it where two parties genuinely face each other.
examples: The bank's position vis-à-vis its European competitors has improved.
Vis-à-vis the state, a city has only the powers the legislature grants it.
She wanted to know where the department stood vis-à-vis the new funding rules.
The treaty leaves the smaller countries weaker vis-à-vis their neighbors.
Our costs are unremarkable vis-à-vis the rest of the industry.
He was hired to handle the company's dealings vis-à-vis the regulators.

entries.type: fixed topic-limiting phrase — prepositional in effect, taking a noun phrase or an -ing form; the clause is frozen, and when it came to is the only variation it allows
entries.clause: adverbial clause of respect, narrowing the main clause to one topic
entries.pattern: When it comes to [noun phrase], [main clause]. · When it comes to [-ing], [main clause]. · [main clause] when it comes to [noun phrase]. · When it came to [noun phrase], [main clause] (past narrative).
entries.punctuation: Comma after the fronted phrase, always. No comma when it trails the main clause.
entries.meaning: Narrows the sentence to a single subject before the claim arrives — "on the topic of." It reads as speech written down: useful in a column or an email, and usually deletable in formal prose, where As for or a plain preposition does the same work in fewer words. Note that it is not a time clause at all, despite the when: nothing in it points to a moment.
examples: When it comes to paperwork, she is the most patient person I know.
When it comes to raising rates, the board has been cautious.
He's fearless on the water and useless when it comes to spiders.
When it came to naming a successor, the founder stalled for two years.
When it comes to barbecue, everyone in this town has a theory and a cousin.
The company is generous with equipment and stingy when it comes to time off.

entries.type: subordinating
entries.register: formal to neutral; the "given that" sense is legal
entries.clause: adverbial clause of contrast, comparing two parallel facts
entries.pattern: [main clause], whereas [clause]. · Whereas [clause], [main clause]. · [X] [verb phrase], whereas [Y] [verb phrase] (the balanced pair). · Whereas [clause]; whereas [clause]; now, therefore, [main clause] (legal preamble).
entries.punctuation: Comma before whereas even when it follows the main clause — unlike most subordinators it is always supplementary, never integral. Comma after the clause when it is fronted. In legal preambles, where each Whereas clause is a separate recital, the recitals are closed with semicolons rather than commas. Note that whereas is a subordinator, not a conjunctive adverb: the comma before it is correct and no semicolon is needed. Write however the other way — We were late; however, they held our table — because that one is an adverb, not a conjunction.
entries.meaning: Sets two facts side by side to point out that they differ, so the contrast is the entire content of the comparison. Compare its neighbors: although concedes, meaning the main clause wins the argument, while whereas balances, asserting both halves equally; and while is ambiguous between "at the same time" and "by contrast," where whereas can only mean the contrast. Note that whilst is British — it is a synonym of while, not of whereas, and it has no place in American prose.
examples: My brother loves horror movies, whereas I can't get through the trailer.
The northern route is faster, whereas the coastal road is prettier.
Whereas the first draft ran long, the second barely filled ten pages.
She was trained as a chemist, whereas her partner came up through sales.
Enrollment rose in the suburbs, whereas the city schools lost students.
Whereas the parties wish to settle all outstanding claims, the following terms are agreed.

entries.type: subordinating — contrast here, but the same word also subordinates time and concession, and outside the conjunction system it is a noun (stay a while) and a verb (while away an afternoon)
entries.register: neutral; a step below whereas in formality and far commoner in speech
entries.clause: adverbial clause of contrast, setting two parallel facts side by side
entries.pattern: [main clause], while [clause]. · While [clause], [main clause]. · [X] [verb phrase], while [Y] [verb phrase] (the balanced pair). · [subject], while [reduced phrase], [predicate] (concessive reduction: The plan, while ambitious, is affordable — see while (concession)).
entries.punctuation: Comma before a trailing contrastive while clause and after a fronted one. That comma is doing real work, because a trailing temporal while clause takes no comma: He waited while she made the call means "during," and He waited, while she made the call means "she, by contrast, made the call." Do not reach for a semicolon here — while is a subordinator, not a conjunctive adverb, so a comma is the correct mark; it is simply not optional in the contrast sense.
entries.meaning: Three jobs, one word: time ("during"), concession ("although"), and contrast ("whereas"). Only context and that comma sort them out, which is why careful American writers switch to whereas whenever a sentence could be read two ways. In the contrast sense while balances two facts and leaves both standing, exactly as whereas does, but at a conversational level. Note that the British whilst is a synonym of while in all three senses, not of whereas, and it has no place in American prose; the same flag applies to amongst and amidst.
examples: The morning session ran long, while the afternoon finished early.
While the coasts get the coverage, the growth is happening inland.
Her first album was all guitars, while this one is mostly synths.
While federal law caps the fee, the state sets no limit at all.
Deliveries are up, while the number of drivers has barely moved.
He handles the money, while she does everything else.
